newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO try to break Hebron impasse.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO try to break Hebron impasse.

text.p: Israeli and Palestinian negotiators worked late into the night to break an impasse on a long-delayed Israeli troop redeployment from the West Bank town of Hebron.

Top Israeli and PLO negotiators held informal talks in a Jerusalem hotel late on Tuesday, labouring in separate U.S.-mediated channels to surmount security and civilian problems blocking agreement on implementing the Hebron deal.
A senior PLO official said formal talks, delayed for two days to allow progress through informal channels, were to resume Wednesday afternoon in the Egyptian seaside resort of Taba.

Palestinians and Israelis offered sharply different views on Tuesday on whether the talks, which began with an American initiative after fierce clashes killed 60 Arabs and 15 Israelis in September, had made headway.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said talks had been fruitless, but Israeli officials said good progress had been made and dismissed Arafat's pessimism as a negotiating tactic.
"Until now, there is no progress in any of the committees in the negotiations," Arafat told reporters in autonomous Jericho at a joint press conference with Jordan's King Hussein.
King Hussein met Arafat in the West Bank for nearly four hours on Tuesday in the Jordanian monarch's first visit to the territory he once ruled since Israel seized it the 1967 war.
Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy told reporters in Jerusalem he hoped outstanding issues on Hebron could be resolved this week. "We are advancing," Levy said.
"There's been very good progress in the talks," Netanyahu's media adviser David Bar-Illan told CNN television.

But U.S. officials in Washington made clear they believed Israeli officials were exaggerating the progress. "Despite what the Israelis are saying, there's been no breakthrough in the talks," one official said.
Bar-Illan said Palestinian pessimism was purely tactical.
"It is a Palestinian tactic which we are familiar with...to create a crisis at the very last minute and to bring in something as astonishing as that idea of American troops."
Arafat said he was ready for U.S. troops to join an international force to guard the 400 Jewish settlers in Hebron, a city of 100,000 Arabs, to calm Israeli security fears.

Bar-Illan said the proposal "may actually cause the deaths of American soldiers in this area and I doubt very much whether bringing home American troops to America in body bags is going to...further...the peace process".
In Washington, U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said the idea to send American forces to Hebron was "not under active consideration".
Arafat was due to travel to Cairo on Wednesday to brief Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak on the negotiations. The Palestinian President held talks with King Hussein in Amman earlier in the week.
King Hussein, Israel's closest Arab ally since making peace in 1994, has lately distanced himself from Netanyahu, who took office in June vowing a tougher line.

"We want to see a speeding up of the implementation of everything that had been agreed upon and to continue until we achieve a just and lasting peace on the Palestinian-Israeli track," the king told reporters in Jericho.
Arabs view Netanyahu's implementation of the Hebron pullback agreed to by Israel's previous government as a litmus test of the right-wing prime minister's peace intentions.
Netanyahu seeks modifications in the accord to better safeguard the Jewish settlers in Hebron's centre. Palestinians refuse to reopen the signed deal.
Israel pulled back its tanks encircling self-ruled Nablus on Tuesday, lifting its blockade of the last West Bank city still under siege since the September clashes.
